title: How hot is the Moon's soil near its south pole?
blurb: India's Chandrayaan-3 pushed a heat probe into the Moon's soil. A gentle slope made the ground much hotter than expected, a clue for finding ice.

source.title: India Bags the Credit for First-Ever In-Situ Measurement of the Topmost Fluffy Layer of the Moon’s Surface at Southern Higher Latitudes
source.license: facts retold in our own words

original.title: Higher surface temperatures near south polar region of the Moon measured by ChaSTE experiment on-board Chandrayaan-3
original.authors: K. Durga Prasad, Chandan Kumar, G. Ambily, P. Kalyana Reddy, Sanjeev K. Mishra and others, with Anil Bhardwaj

cards.b: The Moon has no air to hold heat, so its ground gets very hot by day and very cold at night. Before India's Chandrayaan-3 mission, only two earlier missions, Apollo 15 and 17, had measured temperatures inside the Moon's ground. Both were near the Moon's middle. Nobody had measured the top few centimetres near a pole. How hot does it get there? And could ice hide nearby?

Chandrayaan-3 was a Moon mission of India's space agency, ISRO. A team from the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad, ISRO, and the Space Physics Laboratory in Thiruvananthapuram made an instrument called ChaSTE, which measures the temperature of the ground. The team includes K. Durga Prasad and Anil Bhardwaj. ChaSTE rode on the Vikram lander, which landed in August 2023. They published the results in March 2025.

Vikram landed at a spot named Shiv Shakti point. ChaSTE then pushed a probe 10 centimetres into the soil. The probe has 10 temperature sensors along its length, like marks on a ruler, so it can tell how hot each depth is. From 24 August to 2 September 2023, about 10 Earth days, it measured about once every second. Another sensor, about a metre away on flat ground, measured too.

img.alt: A mosaic of the Moon's south polar region made from about 1,500 pictures by the Clementine spacecraft

cards.b: The soil where the probe went in reached 355 kelvin, which is about 82°C. Kelvin is a temperature scale that scientists use. Orbiting spacecraft had predicted only about 330 kelvin, or 57°C. The reason: the probe sat on ground tilted about 6 degrees towards the Sun. The flat ground a metre away reached about 59°C. So near the poles, temperatures can change a lot within a few steps.

These are real measurements, but from one spot and over only part of one Moon day. A computer model built by the Physical Research Laboratory agrees with them. The idea about ice comes from that model, not from the measurements. Nobody has found ice at these places yet. Future missions will need to dig there to find out.

The model suggests something exciting. Slopes tilted more than 14 degrees towards the pole could stay cold enough to keep water ice, perhaps a few tens of centimetres down. Such places are easier to reach than the poles themselves. Knowing how heat moves through Moon soil also helps engineers plan safe places for people to live.

img.alt: A Moon crater seen by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, which found a little more hydrogen on slopes facing the south pole

cards.b: The probe found that ground tilted towards the Sun gets hotter. Test this on a sunny windowsill. Put a small square of chocolate on each of two pieces of cardboard. Leave one card flat. Prop the other up on a slipper so it faces the Sun. After 10 minutes, which chocolate is softer? Then tilt a card away from the Sun and try again. What do you see?

If there is ice on the Moon, people may one day melt it for water. Should the Moon's ice belong to whichever country reaches it first? Or should it belong to everyone on Earth? How would you share it fairly?
